title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial to measure whether constrained prompting combined with a deterministic generate→verify→repair loop (one allowed repair) increases deterministic-verifier semantic-correctness when translating operator natural-language intents into low-level device configurations. Design: N=150 synthetic intents from a deterministic generator; execution semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial sampled candidate reused across conditions), model = gpt-5-mini, deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, one initial generation per intent and ≤1 repair call permitted. Results (artifact-grounded): baseline = 149/150 (99.333%); guarded = 150/150 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.006667 (≈0.67 percentage points); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Provider accounting: completed episodes = 300; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations = 1. Interpretation: on this preregistered synthetic corpus and under shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded workflow produced a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement over a near-ceiling baseline. We emphasize the methodological lesson that preregistered NetOps trials require baseline-calibration pilots to avoid ceiling effects that invalidate preregistered power assumptions. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the supplied execution bundle referenced by the execution manifest.

sections.introduction:
Natural-language intent interfaces aim to reduce operator burden by letting humans express desired network changes as free text that is automatically translated into executable device configurations. Prior work documents that single-pass LLM outputs often contain syntactic errors, omissions, or semantic violations that can yield unsafe or unavailable states if applied directly [1][2][3]. A commonly proposed defense is a generate→verify→repair architecture in which an LLM produces a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks intent-level invariants or formalized constraints, and an automated repair (or human gate) corrects violations before execution [4][5]. Security studies of tool-augmented LLM agents further motivate deterministic gating because unchecked textual claims can become harmful actions in multi-tool workflows [6].

Research question. After an autonomous literature review and preregistration we posed a confined confirmatory question: does constrained prompting (structured templates with explicit semantic slots) combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase verifier-level semantic correctness of NL→configuration translation versus an unconstrained baseline under a paired design? The trial (study_cand_2026_b2_v1) was preregistered and frozen before any model outputs were observed.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifactized paired confirmatory trial measuring deterministic-verifier pass/fail on a programmatically generated synthetic corpus (N=150 paired intents). (2) Artifact-backed outcomes showing that, under shared_initial_candidate semantics and a one-repair budget, the guarded pipeline raised verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (+0.67 pp), a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). (3) A methodological recommendation that preregistered NetOps trials include baseline-calibration pilots and explicitly specify generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate vs independent sampling) because semantics materially change the estimand and interpretation.
sections.related_work:
Related literature spans intent-translation evaluations, verifier-guided repair systems, formal verifier tooling, and agentic/tool-augmented safety analyses. Multiple recent studies evaluating NL→configuration pipelines report that translating underspecified operator language into verifier-sound artifacts is challenging in practice, with modest semantic-correctness rates reported on heterogeneous task banks [1].

Systems that integrate deterministic verification into generation workflows (policy-guided feedback, verifier-in-the-loop fine-tuning) have shown practical correctness improvements for IaC and configuration repair; effect sizes vary with baseline competence, verifier expressiveness, repair budget, and sampling semantics [2][3]. Formal verification engines (NetKAT/KATch family and related tools) are mature oracles for reachability and isolation checks and are often used as gating layers in LLM-driven NetOps workflows [5]. Security analyses of agentic LLM pipelines document claim-to-action and prompt-injection vulnerabilities that motivate conservative, auditable verifier gating in multi-tool deployments [4].

Our trial intentionally emphasizes preregistration, paired inference, and deterministic-verifier endpoints while making explicit the experimental knobs (sampling semantics and repair budget) that prior work identifies as consequential.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory design. The study was preregistered as study_cand_2026_b2_v1 with a frozen analysis plan executed before any model outputs were observed. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline evaluated with an exact two-sided McNemar test on deterministic-verifier pass/fail outcomes. The confirmatory sample specified N=150 distinct synthetic intents drawn deterministically from a preregistered generator, deterministic inclusion/exclusion rules, a deterministic retry policy for provider timeouts, and a power target to detect an absolute +15 percentage-point improvement with ≈80% power under conservative discordant-pair assumptions. All preregistered elements (estimands, inclusion/exclusion rules, multiplicity plan, and analysis scripts) were frozen and archived prior to model calls.

Conceptual preregistered arms vs executed contrast (required clarification). The preregistration described a conceptual three-arm design: A = baseline free-text prompting, B = constrained-template prompting, and C = constrained + verifier-feedback (generate→verify→repair). The archived execution, however, enforced shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent the adapter produced exactly one initial sampled candidate that was reused across paired evaluations of baseline (A) and guarded (C). Under this enforcement constrained-only (B) was not executed as an independent first-pass condition and therefore no confirmatory B vs A or C vs B contrasts are reported from the archived run. Consequently the reported primary estimand corresponds specifically to the marginal effect of applying at most one repair to the identical initial candidate (C vs A under shared_initial_candidate semantics). This mapping from preregistration labels to the executed contrast is explicit in the archived execution manifest (stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 150, repair: 1}) and in the analysis artifacts.

Execution semantics, model, and deterministic validator. The adapter enforced the shared_initial_candidate execution semantics and the repair budget (≤1 repair per intent). Declared model: gpt-5-mini (provider record: openai_responses); model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null (unset). No numeric temperature or fixed random-seed was enforced, so independent-session nondeterminism remains possible and was anticipated in the preregistration. Deterministic verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied a full_intent_constraint_validation rule and returned a boolean pass/fail plus detailed per-episode diagnostics; these verifier verdicts constitute the binary endpoint.

Task generator and prechecks. Confirmatory tasks were produced deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and stratified across four intent families with topologies limited to 4–32 nodes for verifier coverage. Parser and mapping unit-tests required by the preregistration were run before batch execution and passed. Inclusion/exclusion rules (ambiguity detector, parse failures, unsupported verifier features) were applied deterministically prior to any model call; no confirmatory exclusions occurred in the archived run.

Primary analysis procedures and preregistration adherence. The primary analysis is the exact two-sided McNemar test on the paired contingency (n_11, n_10, n_01, n_00) with a paired bootstrap-percentile 95% CI from 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistered handling of incomplete pairs (exclude from primary test) and multiplicity corrections for secondary contrasts were preserved; because B was not run as an independent first-pass condition under the archived execution, no confirmatory B vs A or C vs B contrasts are reported. No post-preregistration or post-lock changes were made to the confirmatory analysis; reported analyses follow the archived paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor and the frozen analysis plan.
sections.results:
Execution and provider audit. The run completed as planned: completed_episode_count = 300 and complete_pair_count = 150. Provider-call accounting: model_calls_used = 151; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 151; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0; cache_miss_count = 151. Stage-level counts: shared_initial_generation = 150 and repair = 1. No contamination flags or pre-execution unit-test failures occurred.

Primary numerical outcomes and contingency counts. Paired contingency counts (guarded × baseline): n_11 = 149 (both-pass), n_10 = 1 (guarded-only-pass), n_01 = 0 (baseline-only-pass), n_00 = 0 (both-fail). Per-condition success rates: baseline_success_count = 149/150 = 0.9933333333333333; guarded_success_count = 150/150 = 1.0. Estimated paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00666666666666671 (≈0.67 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). These figures are reported verbatim from the archived analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv).

Discordant pair and repair diagnostics. Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150), consistent with the near-ceiling initial success rate; the single discordant pair corresponds to pair-000069 in the archived raw results. That single repair converted one initially invalid candidate to a valid configuration under the deterministic verifier. Median revision iterations for guarded episodes = 0 (IQR = 0). Representative validator traces and normalized_configuration strings for tasks 000001–000006 are archived and illustrate validator diagnostics (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes).

Power calibration note (required clarification). The preregistered power target—designed to detect an absolute improvement of +15 percentage points at ≈80% power—was invalidated by the observed baseline_success_rate ≈99.33%. The very low number of discordant pairs (n_10 + n_01 = 1) provides limited information for the McNemar test; this ceiling effect reduces the trial's ability to demonstrate the preregistered detectable effect. No post-lock modifications to the confirmatory analysis were performed; all reported results follow the archived preregistered analysis plan.
sections.discussion:
Ceiling effect and implications for preregistration. The observed near-ceiling baseline (≈99.33%) left almost no headroom for the guarded repair to show a large absolute improvement and therefore invalidated the preregistered detectable-effect assumptions. We recommend baseline-calibration pilots (20–40 tasks sampled from the planned generator and prompt style) to estimate baseline competence and adjust confirmatory N or task difficulty before committing to final sampling. The archived task generator seeds and representative tasks permit such a pilot reproducibly.

Sampling semantics and estimand trade-offs. The shared_initial_candidate semantics used here isolates the marginal effect of repairing an identical sampled candidate (C vs A). Alternative semantics (independent per-condition sampling or multi-draw budgets) estimate different operational questions and typically require more model calls and different power planning. Practitioners should match sampling semantics to deployment constraints (single-pass action vs resampling) and include model-call cost in power calculations.

Operational affordances beyond pass/fail. Deterministic validators provide structured diagnostics (violation codes, normalized configurations) that assist human triage and audit even when pass/fail differences are small; these operational benefits complement binary endpoints and are preserved in the archived artifacts.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: adapter-enforced budgets and unit-tests mitigated cross-condition leakage. Construct validity: verifier pass/fail is a proxy for semantic correctness and depends on mapping code and verifier coverage. External validity: single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic small topologies (4–32 nodes) limit generalization to production WANs and other models. Security: adversarial prompt-injection was not evaluated and remains a separate concern requiring targeted adversary-driven experiments.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory trial comparing baseline free-text prompting with constrained-template prompting plus a single verifier-guided repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. On a deterministic synthetic corpus with gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the guarded pipeline increased verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (≈0.67 pp), a numerically tiny and statistically non-significant difference (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). The principal scientific lesson is methodological: preregistered NetOps trials should include baseline calibration to avoid ceiling effects and preserve statistical power. Technically, our artifacts bound the marginal benefit of a one-repair guarded pipeline under shared_initial_candidate semantics; evaluating independent-sampling semantics, larger repair budgets, model diversity, and production-scale topologies remains important future work.

Execution semantics and mapping to preregistered arms: the preregistration described conceptual arms A (baseline), B (constrained), and C (guarded); the archived run enforced shared_initial_candidate semantics so that a single initial candidate per intent was reused across baseline (A) and guarded (C), and B was not executed as an independent first-pass condition—hence the primary confirmatory contrast reported is C vs A under shared_initial_candidate semantics. No human manually edited technical content, analyses, figures, captions, or references after the autonomy lock. All runtime sampling metadata, provider-call traces, verifier inputs/verdicts, and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle referenced by the execution manifest. Finally, the preregistered power target (detecting +15 percentage points) was invalidated by the observed baseline ≈99.33%; the confirmatory analysis reported here follows the frozen preregistration and no post-lock modifications were made to the primary analysis.
limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to at most one guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or multiple-repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than the pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned detectable effect = 15 percentage points), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures deterministic validator pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
